analysis.one_liner: Requires the SEC to prove each new rule's benefits outweigh its costs before adopting it.
analysis.headline: The House passed the SEC Regulatory Accountability Act 235-161 on May 17, 2013, but the Senate Banking Committee never took it up, and the bill died when that Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten how the Securities and Exchange Commission writes rules. Before adopting any rule, the SEC would have had to show, with cost-benefit analysis overseen by its Chief Economist, that the rule's benefits justify its costs, and it would have had to periodically review existing rules for repeal. Supporters called it accountability for an overly aggressive regulator; the practical effect would have been to make financial rules — including investor protections — slower to adopt, harder to defend, and easier for regulated firms to challenge.
analysis.who_benefits: Securities firms, public companies, and other regulated market participants, who would face a higher bar for every SEC rule, periodic chances to have existing rules streamlined or repealed, and new procedural grounds to challenge rules they disliked. Smaller public companies were specifically singled out for relief from a Sarbanes-Oxley audit requirement.

how_it_helps.text: Before issuing any regulation, the SEC would have to identify the problem the rule addresses, use its Chief Economist to assess costs and benefits, and adopt the rule only on a 'reasoned determination that the benefits of the intended regulation justify the costs.'

The SEC would have to weigh whether each rulemaking promotes efficiency, competition, and capital formation, and consider the rule's impact on investor choice, market liquidity, and small businesses, while choosing the approach that imposes the least burden on society and market participants.

The SEC would have to review its existing regulations every five years and modify, streamline, or repeal any that are 'outmoded, ineffective, insufficient, or excessively burdensome,' with the review directed to specifically weigh the burden of Sarbanes-Oxley internal-control audit requirements on companies with a public float of $250 million or less.

For each 'major rule,' the SEC would have to publish an assessment plan, including an analysis of jobs added or lost split between public and private sectors, and within 180 days of the assessment either propose amending or rescinding the rule or formally determine no action is needed.

Rules adopted by the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board and registered securities associations such as FINRA could not take effect unless the SEC determined they complied with the new cost-benefit requirements.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary investors, especially retirement savers, who rely on SEC rules for honest disclosures, anti-fraud enforcement, and fair markets. Investor-protection benefits are diffuse and hard to quantify, so a strict cost-benefit showing would fall hardest on exactly the rules designed to protect them, and repealed or blocked rules would shift risk back onto the people buying stocks, bonds, and funds.

drawbacks.text: The bill would require the SEC to demonstrate, before adopting any rule, that quantified benefits justify quantified costs [S5]. For anti-fraud, disclosure, and market-integrity rules, the benefits — losses that never happen — are inherently difficult to measure, so this standard could delay or block investor protections without proving them wasteful.

The bill would direct the SEC to periodically review rules for repeal and to specifically weigh the burden of Sarbanes-Oxley internal-control attestation on companies with a public float of $250 million or less [S5]. Weaker internal-control audits mean investors get less assurance that the financial statements they rely on are accurate.

The bill's instruction to choose the regulatory approach that 'maximizes net benefits' and imposes the 'least burden' on market participants would legally require the SEC to weigh industry compliance costs against investor protection in every rule [S5], a trade-off that has historically favored the parties with the best-funded cost arguments.

Requiring SEC certification before any rule of the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board or FINRA could take effect would add a procedural layer that could stall municipal-market and broker-conduct rules even where no one disputes their substance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a genuine good-faith case for the bill: SEC rules do impose real compliance costs, and better economic analysis, plain-language drafting, and periodic review of outmoded rules can make regulation sharper rather than weaker. But the bill's core mechanism — a mandatory showing that benefits justify costs for every rule, with repeal reviews and jobs accounting — is aimed at making rules easier to stop, and the parties best positioned to exploit that are the regulated firms themselves. The cost of slower or weaker investor protection falls on ordinary savers who have no seat in the comment-letter process, so the drawbacks outweigh the procedural gains.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the House on a mostly party-line vote, but after the Senate received it on May 20, 2013, the Banking Committee never brought it to a vote, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced by Representative Scott Garrett on March 12, 2013 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee.
The committee ordered the bill reported on a 31-28 vote and reported it on May 13, 2013.
The House passed the bill 235-161 on May 17, 2013, with 218 of 232 voting Republicans in favor and 161 of 201 voting Democrats opposed; 17 Democrats joined the Republicans.
An amendment by Representative Maxine Waters to recommit the bill with investor-protection instructions failed 179-217, with 216 of 232 Republicans voting no and 178 of 201 Democrats voting yes.
The Senate received the bill on May 20, 2013 and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, where no further action was taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary investors came out ahead. Because the Senate never acted, the SEC kept its existing rulemaking authority — including the investor-protection and disclosure rules being written after the 2008 financial crisis — intact and unencumbered by the new cost-benefit and repeal mandates. The securities industry did not get the lighter regulatory environment the bill would have created.

for.name: Scott Garrett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, and as a Financial Services Committee member saw it through markup, committee report, and House passage.

for.name: 218 of 232 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on final passage, 218-0 among voting Republicans.

for.name: Jeb Hensarling
for.what_they_did: His committee marked up the bill, ordered it reported 31-28, and sent it to the floor within two months of introduction.

against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the House-passed bill in his committee on May 20, 2013 and never scheduled it for a markup or a Senate vote.

against.name: 161 of 201 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage, 161-17 among voting Democrats.

against.name: Maxine Waters
against.role: Ranking Member, House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill with instructions to add investor-protection language; the motion failed 179-217.

sides.party_line_note: On final passage, 218 of 232 voting Republicans voted yes while 161 of 201 voting Democrats voted no, with 17 Democrats crossing over; the committee vote was likewise 31-28 along party lines.

industries.note: The bill would make every SEC rule harder to adopt and easier to challenge for failing a cost-benefit test, cutting compliance costs for the very firms those rules police. The resulting risk of weaker anti-fraud and disclosure rules would fall on ordinary investors.

Periodic review and possible repeal of 'excessively burdensome' rules — with the Sarbanes-Oxley internal-control audit for companies under $250 million in public float specifically flagged — would lower disclosure and audit costs while giving investors less assurance that reported financials are reliable.

industries.industry: Securities self-regulators (FINRA, Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board)
industries.note: Their rules could not take effect without an SEC certification that they met the new cost-benefit requirements, adding procedural delay but also imposing the same analytical discipline on their rulemaking.
